content: 1. Testing for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis, and bacterial vaginosis should be conducted. If antimicrobial resistance testing for N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium is available, it should be performed. In the absence of such testing at primary healthcare centers, referral to a specialist in sexually transmitted infections or a gynecologist is recommended. 2. Mothers living with HIV are advised to breastfeed their infants for at least 12 months and may continue breastfeeding for up to 24 months or longer, similar to recommendations for the general population. This should be done while ensuring full support for adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life, followed by the introduction of appropriate complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding. Breastfeeding should only cease when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. 3. ART significantly reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in the context of mixed feeding. While exclusive breastfeeding is recommended, mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ART is being administered. 4. If mothers living with HIV do not plan to breastfeed for 12 months, shorter durations of breastfeeding are still beneficial compared to not breastfeeding at all. 5. Following an HIV diagnosis, a package of support interventions should be offered to ensure timely linkage to care. These interventions include enhanced case management, support for HIV disclosure, tracing, staff training to provide multiple services, and streamlined service delivery. 6. ART initiation should follow principles of people-centered care, which prioritize the health needs, preferences, and dignity of individuals. People newly diagnosed with HIV should be retested to confirm their status before starting ART to minimize the risk of misdiagnosis. 7. The treat all recommendation supports rapid ART initiation for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count. Same-day ART initiation should be offered to those ready to start, especially for individuals with advanced HIV disease. 8. Clinical visits for individuals established on ART should occur every 3–6 months, preferably every six months if feasible. ART refills should also last 3–6 months, with six-month refills being ideal if supply management allows. 9. Adherence support interventions, such as peer counseling, mobile phone text reminders, cognitive behavioral therapy, and fixed-dose combination regimens, should be provided to individuals on ART to improve adherence and virological suppression. 10. Community support programs should be implemented to improve retention in HIV care. These may include community-based interventions, adherence clubs, and additional care for high-risk individuals. 11. HIV programs should implement tracing and re-engagement interventions for individuals who have disengaged from care. 12. Task sharing for ART initiation and maintenance is recommended. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate and maintain ART. Community health workers and lay providers can dispense ART under supervision. 13. Decentralization of ART care should be considered to improve access and retention. ART initiation can occur in hospitals, with maintenance at peripheral health facilities or community levels. 14. ART should be initiated and maintained in maternal and child healthcare settings for pregnant and postpartum women and infants, with appropriate linkage to ongoing HIV care. 15. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings, and TB treatment may be provided in HIV care settings for individuals diagnosed with both conditions. 16. Sexual and reproductive health services, including contraception and STI management, may be integrated into HIV care settings to improve service delivery. 17. Diabetes and hypertension care may also be integrated into HIV services to address comorbidities effectively. 18. ART should be initiated and maintained in care settings providing opioid substitution therapy (OST) for individuals living with HIV. 19. Disease programs, particularly for HIV and TB, should work towards balanced integration of diagnostic services to improve care delivery. 20. Adolescent-friendly services should be implemented within HIV care to ensure engagement and improved outcomes for adolescents living with HIV. Psychosocial interventions should also be provided to support adolescents and young adults living with HIV. 21. Electronic communication systems can be used to transfer laboratory test results, such as those for infant HIV diagnosis, to reduce delays in acting on critical results.
